title: Comparison Operators and Conditions
learningObjectives: Explain comparison operators as tools for comparing values.
Distinguish JavaScript strict equality from coercive equality.
Express requirement boundaries accurately using comparisons.
Recognize type, unit and floating-point comparison pitfalls.

understand.concept: Comparison operators examine two values and produce a logical result. Relational comparisons test whether a value is less than or greater than another, including boundary-inclusive forms. Equality comparisons test whether values are equal according to the language's rules. Operator syntax and type-conversion behaviour vary between languages.
understand.whyItMatters: Comparisons turn requirements into testable conditions used in eligibility checks, ranges, searching, sorting, validation and branching. Incorrect operator choice can create bugs at boundaries or with mismatched types.
understand.analogy: A shopkeeper compares a customer's available amount with the price. The comparison gives a logical answer used to decide whether the purchase can proceed.
understand.analogyLimit: Real prices can include tax, currency precision, discounts and unavailable data. Comparisons assume values are valid and expressed in compatible units.

explain.narrative: Comparison operators include less than (<), greater than (>), less than or equal to (<=), and greater than or equal to (>=). Equality and inequality syntax varies by language. In JavaScript, === and !== compare without equality coercion; == and != may convert values. For example, 5 === '5' is false, while 5 == '5' is true. Prefer strict equality in most JavaScript code unless coercion is intentional and understood. Translate requirement wording carefully: “under 10” usually means value < 10; “10 or under” means value <= 10; “at least 10” means value >= 10; “exactly 10” means an equality test. Test the threshold itself, and values just below and above it. Comparisons alone do not validate data: numeric text may need parsing, and units must be normalized before comparing. Computed floating-point decimals can have rounding representation differences; exact equality is often inappropriate for computed values. Use a tolerance or an appropriate representation, such as integer minor currency units, when the domain requires it. Common errors include omitting equality at a boundary, using coercive equality accidentally, comparing unparsed text, comparing different units, and assuming all languages use identical rules.

examples.title: Relational boundary
examples.explanation: 70 is not greater than 70, but it is greater than or equal to 70.

examples.title: Strict and coercive equality
examples.explanation: Strict equality does not convert the string to a number; loose equality performs coercion in this comparison.

examples.title: Inclusive range check
examples.code: const t = 22; const ok = t >= 18 && t <= 26; console.log(ok);
examples.explanation: 22 is within the inclusive range 18 to 26. Combining conditions is explored further in F2.3.

examples.title: Unit mismatch
examples.code: const km = 5; const meters = 4000; console.log(km > meters);
examples.explanation: JavaScript compares the numeric values, but the comparison is meaningless because kilometers and meters were not converted to a common unit.

examples.title: Floating-point caution
examples.explanation: Binary floating-point representation makes the computed sum slightly different from 0.3; a tolerance check is suitable for this demonstration.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Passing score boundary
guidedTask.instructions: A learner qualifies with a score of 70 or above. Use scores 69, 70 and 71. Predict each result for score >= 70 before running the code.
steps: Translate “70 or above” into a comparison.
guidedTask.starterCode: const score = 70; const qualifies = score >= 70; console.log(qualifies);

independentTask.title: Independent: Temperature range
independentTask.instructions: Create a Boolean check for a value from 10 through 30 inclusive. Test 9, 10, 20, 30 and 31. Explain why the endpoints are included.
requirements: Explain the expected result for each case.

hints: Translate the boundary phrase before choosing an operator.
At least includes the threshold; greater than does not.
Consider whether strict equality is intended in JavaScript.
Test below, at and above each boundary.
Normalize types and units before comparing.

questions.prompt: Which operator means less than or equal to?
questions.explanation: <= includes values smaller than the boundary and the boundary itself.
Strict equality does not convert a number to a string for this comparison.

questions.prompt: Which comparison includes a person who is exactly 18 when the rule says minimum age 18?
Why is directly comparing 5 kilometers with 4000 meters logically incorrect?
options: Convert both values to the same unit first
questions.answer: Convert both values to the same unit first
questions.explanation: A meaningful comparison requires compatible units.

questions.prompt: Why can exact equality be unreliable for computed floating-point decimals?
options: Some decimal fractions are not represented exactly in binary floating point
questions.answer: Some decimal fractions are not represented exactly in binary floating point
questions.explanation: A suitable tolerance or domain-appropriate representation is needed when exact decimal equality matters.
